title: Game 1: Magnus vs Hans
notes: Game 1 of 12 in the experiment, from the Ruy Lopez. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

This is a Spanish setup where the bishop retreated to a4 instead of staying on b5, so castling is the natural developing move that keeps the king safe and prepares Re1 or d4. I checked 5...Nxe4 6.Re1 d5 7.Nxe5 Nxe5 8.Rxe5+, which regains the material favourably, so castling loses nothing.

This is the main-line Spanish; I can grab the pawn with Nxe4 (Open Variation), but that invites sharp complications after 6.d4 b5 7.Bb3 d5. I prefer the solid Closed setup with Be7, preparing to castle and support e5 while keeping my structure sound.

This is the main-line Closed Ruy Lopez; Re1 defends e4 and sets up the Bxc6/Nxe5 trick, so Black must respond with ...b5. Alternatives like Nxe5 fail to ...Nxe5 followed by tactics, and Bxc6 just concedes the bishop pair.

White's bishop on a4 is awkwardly placed, so 6...b5 hits it with tempo and gains space; 7.Bxb5 axb5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Rxe5 gives up a bishop for only two pawns, and 7.Nxe5 Nxe5 8.Rxe5 bxa4 just loses a piece. I preferred this to 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe5 Nxe5 8.Rxe4, which only simplifies without winning material.
My bishop on a4 is attacked by the b5 pawn; Bxb5 axb5 Nxb5 only wins two pawns for a piece, so I retreat to the strong diagonal with Bb3, keeping pressure on f7 and eyeing d5.

Castling is the safest developing move here; grabbing with Nxe4 lets White recover after 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Rxe4 with my king still in the centre, and 7...Nxe4 8.Rxe4 d5 9.Rxe5 Nxe5 10.Nxe5 leaves me a pawn down. After 7...O-O, 8.Nxe5?? simply loses a piece since the e4 pawn blocks the rook's recapture on e5.

Black has castled without playing d6, so 8.c3 would allow the Marshall Attack with 8...d5; instead I play the anti-Marshall 8.a4, immediately pressuring b5 while e4 stays defended by my rook (so 8...Nxe4 9.Rxe4 d5 10.Re1 simply drops a piece). After 8...b4 or 8...Bb7 9.d3 I keep a solid, flexible structure with a queenside initiative.

My e5 pawn is only defended by the knight, so White was threatening Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 winning a clean pawn (and ...d6 would just chase the rook). Playing d6 solidifies the centre, transposing into normal Ruy Lopez structures, and tactics like Bxf7+ followed by Nxe5 don't work since after Rxf7 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 White has given bishop and knight for only knight and two pawns.

I noticed Black's rook on a8 is completely undefended — the bishop on c8 blocks the queen and doesn't cover a8 — so after axb5 axb5 my rook simply takes on a8, and even Black's best 9...Na5 10.bxa6 Nxb3 11.cxb3 Bxa6 leaves me a pawn up with an open a-file. I checked the alternative 9.c3 (solid but releases the pressure on a6) and Black's tricks like 9...Nxe4 10.Rxe4 d5 11.Rxe5, which also favour me.

White has just captured on b5, so I simply recapture to restore material balance and keep my strong pawn chain; the tactic 10.Nxe5 Nxe5 11.Rxe5 fails to 11...dxe5 winning a rook for a knight. Recapturing with the pawn also keeps my c6 knight active and opens the a-file for my rook.

I checked the recapture possibilities on a8 and found that nothing defends Black's rook there — the c8 bishop doesn't cover a8, and both the queen and the f8 rook are blocked along the eighth rank, so Rxa8 simply wins a whole rook. I also verified that the tempting Nxe5 fails because after Nxe5 Rxe5, the d6 pawn captures the rook.

My rook was taken on a8 and I'm not offered Bxa8, so White's rook will simply run down the a-file (a7/a5 are covered by my knight, a6 by my bishop, a4 by my b-pawn) — I can't trap it. So I grab the loose e4 pawn with Nxe4 while the a8 rook is still en prise; if White takes with Rxe4 or defends with Qe2, I win the rook back with Bxa8, and 11.Rxc8 Nxf2 keeps my deficit minimal with a shattered white king.

My rook on a8 is attacked by the bishop on c8, and Black's knight on e4 is completely undefended, so I take the bishop first with Rxc8; after the forced Qxc8 I win the e4 knight with Rxe4, ending up two pieces for a pawn. The alternative Rxe4 immediately allows Bxa8 and only nets a knight for my rook.

The rook on c8 is only attacked by my queen, so any other move allows Rxd8 winning my queen — I must recapture immediately with Qxc8, even though my knight on e4 is then loose to Rxe4. Alternatives like Nxf2 or Nc3 that hit the queen fail to Rxd8 followed by Rxf8+, which is far worse, so recovering the rook is clearly the lesser evil and I'll follow up with d5 and e4 for activity.

Black's 10...Nxe4 was a blunder, so I'm up a bishop for a pawn after the exchanges on a8/c8; the key now is to simply win or evict the loose knight on e4 without giving material back (Rxe4 would return rook for knight, Bxf7+ loses a bishop to Rxf7). The move d3 attacks the knight, and if 12...Nd4 13.Nxd4 exd4 14.dxe4 I just take it, while after 12...Nf6 I keep a clean extra piece plus Nxe5 ideas.

My knight on e4 is attacked by the d3 pawn, so it must move; Nc5 retreats it to a strong square while attacking the b3 bishop and gaining a tempo. Tactical checks: Nxe5 fails to Nxe5, and Bxf7+ Rxf7 gains White nothing, so Nc5 is safe and active.

My bishop on b3 is attacked by the knight on c5, and I'm up a bishop for a pawn, so I just need a safe, active retreat. Bd5 is untouchable (no black piece attacks d5) and it immediately hits the undefended knight on c6, whereas Ba4/Bc4/Be6 all lose the bishop to bxa4, bxc4 or Nxe6, and Nxe5 fails to 13...Nxe5 since b3 hangs.

My c6 knight is attacked by the strong Bd5, so I want a move that both saves it and hits back — Nb4 does exactly that, attacking the bishop (plus c2 and d3) and forcing White to either surrender the bishop for a knight (14.Be4 Ncxe4 15.dxe4, or 14.Bb3 Nxb3) or defend it with 14.Nc3 Nxd5. I checked that Nb4 isn't hit by anything (no a3/c3 pawn yet) and that 14.c3?? would simply drop the bishop to Nxd5, so this is the cleanest way to trade off White's best piece while keeping my extra pawn.

My Bd5 is attacked by Nb4, and d3 is attacked twice (Nb4, Nc5) but defended only by Qd1, so a loose bishop retreat like Bb7 or c3 allows ...Nbxd3! Qxd3 Ncxd3 winning my queen. Be4 both saves the bishop and adds a defender to d3; if ...Nxe4 dxe4 I remain a piece for a pawn ahead with c2 safely guarded.

I'm down a bishop for a pawn, so I need to pose concrete problems rather than simplify — 14...d5 hits the e4 bishop, and almost every capture (15.Bxd5 Nbxd5, 15.Nxe5 dxe4, 15.c3 dxe4, 15.Nc3 dxe4) wins the piece back and levels the material. Tactically it's safe: 15.Bxh7+ Kxh7 16.Ng5+ just loses to Bxg5, so White's only real try is the awkward retreat 15.Bf5, after which 15...g6 leaves me with a strong center and active knights.

My e4 bishop is attacked by the d5 pawn and has no safe retreat (Bf5 loses to Qxf5, Bg6 to fxg6), so I cash it in for pawns: Bxd5 Nxd5 and then Nxe5 nets two pawns for the bishop, leaving me a clean pawn up with equal pieces. Bxh7+ only leads to a roughly level ending after ...Bxg5, so I prefer the material route.

The bishop on d5 is completely undefended — the queen's path down the d-file is blocked by White's own d3 pawn, and no knight, rook or pawn covers that square, so Nb4xd5 simply recovers the piece and restores material equality. The alternative of Qd7 to pile on the bishop just lets it retreat (Bb3/Be4) and leaves me a full piece down. After 15...Nxd5 16.Nxe5 I can play Bd6 or Re8 to hit the knight and stay fully in the game.

I checked every black piece and the e5 pawn is completely undefended — neither knight, the bishop on e7, nor the queen on c8 covers it — while my knight on e5 would be backed by the rook on e1. The counter-tries all fail: Nc5xd3 drops a knight to cxd3, and Nd5-f4 is simply met by Bxf4, so I win a clean pawn.

Material is equal but my pieces are far more active while White's queenside is undeveloped, so I want a move that develops with tempo. Bd6 hits the e5 knight (only defended by Re1) and eyes h2; tactical tries like Nc6 fail to Qxc6 and Ng4 just drops a piece to Qxg4. Immediate Nxd3 loses a knight to cxd3, and Ne3/Ne4 are simply captured by f2/d3 pawns.

I'm a pawn up, and my c-pawn hits both black knights' squares (b5 and d5) at once, gaining time; after 17.c4 Bxe5 18.Rxe5 my rook also attacks the c5 knight, and 17...bxc4 18.dxc4 keeps the extra pawn while any knight retreat allows 18.cxb5 for a second pawn. I checked that Nxd3 ideas fail since d3 stays defended by my queen.

My d5 knight is hit by the c4 pawn, so it must move, and Nb4 is the most active retreat: it joins the knight on c5 in double-attacking d3 while my bishop keeps pressure on the loose Ne5. If White grabs with 18.cxb5 I get counterplay with Qa6/Bxe5 and recover the d3 pawn, and 18.Bf4? even loses to Bxe5 followed by Ncxd3 winning the queen.

Black's two knights were ganging up on d3 (Nbxd3 would win the pawn since Qxd3 runs into Nxd3), so I advance the pawn out of danger with d4, which simultaneously attacks the knight on c5 and leaves b5 hanging to cxb5 next. If Black grabs with Nbd3 anyway, Nxd3 Nxd3 Qxd3 wins a piece, and Bxe5 dxe5 just strengthens my center while I stay a pawn up.

White's 18.d4 hits my c5 knight while c4 hits b5, so I need to resolve the tension before I lose a pawn or piece; capturing on e5 first removes White's strong knight and keeps my ...Ncd3 resource alive (Qxd3 Nxd3 would win the queen), after which ...Nxc1 and ...bxc4 restore material equality. The greedy 18...bxc4 fails to 19.dxc5, so Bxe5 is the cleanest path.

Black's bishop just took on e5 and I can recapture, but dxc5 is better: it takes the knight on c5 while leaving the bishop on e5 still hanging to my Re1, and it removes the knight that would have supported ...Nd3 (now ...Nd3 or ...Nc2 simply loses to Qxd3/Qxc2). After dxc5 Black must spend a move saving the bishop (e.g. Bf6), and material is level with me holding an extra pawn.

My b5 pawn was hanging to cxb5, which would leave me two pawns down, so I grabbed back the pawn to level material. After bxc4 White's natural central tries fail: 20.Qd5 Nxd5 wins the queen (c4 no longer guards d5), 20.Qd4 Bxd4, and 20.Qa4 Nd3! hits Re1/Bc1 while White's queenside pieces stay tangled.

The black bishop on e5 is completely undefended and my rook on e1 hits it down an open file, so Rxe5 simply wins a piece. The only tricky reply is 20...Nd3 forking rook and bishop, but 21.Re3 (or 21.Rxd3 cxd3 22.Qxd3) keeps me clearly up material.

I'm down a bishop, so I need tactics: the rook on e5 is undefended and Nd3 forks it together with the bishop on c1 (also hitting f2 and b2). White can't take with Qxd3 (cxd3 wins the queen) and Rxd3 cxd3 drops the exchange, so after something like Rd5 or Re3 I at least win the bishop back with Nxc1, reducing White's extra material and leaving me a passed c-pawn for counterplay.

My rook on e5 is attacked by the knight on d3, so I must move it, and Re4 is the best square: it stays safe from everything, attacks the undefended c4 pawn (the knight's only defender), and covers the f4 escape square while my queen on d1 already eyes the knight. If Black defends with Qf5 I simply take on c4, staying a piece and a pawn up.

I'm a piece down, so I need to keep my active knight and my c4 pawn alive as compensation. 21...Qa6 defends c4 (stopping Rxc4), keeps the knight on d3 protected by the pawn, and prepares to pick off c5 — whereas immediate 21...Nxc5 22.Rxc4 just restores White's clean extra piece with symmetrical pawns.

I'm a full bishop up, so my priority is keeping everything safe and neutralising the annoying knight on d3. Rd4 attacks the undefended knight while staying safe (Black's c4 pawn can't capture backwards and the queen doesn't cover d4), and every knight capture — Nxc1, Nxb2, Nxf2 — simply loses the piece for me to recapture.

My knight on d3 is hanging to Rd4 (backed by Qd1), so I must move it, and Nxc5 both saves it and grabs a pawn — importantly White can't answer Rxc4 because with the c4 pawn gone my queen on a6 would hit the rook along a6–b5–c4 and win it. The knight on c5 is attacked by nothing immediately, and after Be3 or b4 I have Ne6 or Nb3 (defended by c4) available, so this cuts my material deficit while keeping my pieces active.

I'm up a bishop for a pawn, and I noticed Rxc4 fails because Black's queen guards c4 from a6 (Qxc4), so instead I develop with tempo: Be3 attacks the undefended knight on c5, covers f2, and if Black grabs b2 later (Nd3/Nxb2) I win the knight with Rb4. Black's Nb3 fork try only costs me a tempo (Rd7 hits c7) while my piece advantage stays.

The bishop on e3 doesn't yet hit my knight because White's own rook on d4 blocks the diagonal, but any rook move would uncover that attack, so I want the knight out now with tempo. Nb3 attacks the rook, and the knight is safely defended by my c4 pawn, while Rxc4 would simply lose the rook to Qxc4.

I'm a clean bishop up (Q+R+B+N+4P vs Q+R+N+5P), and my rook on d4 is attacked by the knight on b3, so I must not allow Nxd4 Bxd4 which would hand back the exchange and level material. Rd8 both saves the rook and forces a rook trade (Rxd8 Qxd8+), simplifying into an endgame where my extra piece dominates; if Black declines with Nd4 or Qa1, I simply take on f8 and stay a full rook up in the exchange.

My rook on f8 is attacked by Rd8 and only defended by the king, so I must deal with it — Kh8 or any other move simply drops the rook. Rxd8 allows Qxd8+ with the white queen invading on c7, whereas Re8 either forces 25.Rxe8+ Qxe8 (where my queen gets a good active post and White's queen stays passive) or leaves my rook actively placed on the e-file if White declines; I'm a piece for a pawn down, so I need the most active setup.

Black's rook on e8 is undefended and taking it gives check along the eighth rank; the king on g8 has f8 and h8 covered by the rook and g7/f7/h7 blocked by its own pawns, and nothing can capture or interpose.

new_lessons: [middlegame] When your piece is attacked and a pawn near your king is loose, defend with a developing move (Nc3, Nbd2, Be3) instead of shuffling the attacked piece Example: Move 14 Bd5 was hit by Nb4; Be4 "defended d3" but Nc3 was far better and kept +87%

[middlegame] Before putting a bishop on a central square, check every enemy pawn that can advance to attack it (d5, f5, e5, c5) and verify a safe retreat exists Example: Be4 met ...d5/...f5; the bishop had no square (Bf5 Qxf5, Bg6 fxg6) and was lost for two pawns

[middlegame] Never swap a bishop or knight for two pawns while pieces are active; first search all checks and sacrifices that win the piece back or expose the king Example: Trapped on e4 I played Bxd5 for pawns; Bxh7+ first was stronger and kept more winning chances

[middlegame] With a clear material edge, play the simplest consolidating developing move; avoid clever maneuvers that put pieces on squares pawns can attack Example: A piece up at 87%, Be4 instead of Nc3 threw away most of the advantage in two moves

[opening] Before any exchange sequence on an open file, recount defenders of your central pawn e4/d4 after the trades Example: 8.a4 axb5 9.axb5 Rxa8 allowed 10...Nxe4 because the rook trade cost e4 its guard

[middlegame] When choosing between recaptures, prefer taking the opponent's most active piece over a greedy pawn grab that lets their piece escape with tempo Example: 19.dxc5 instead of Rxe5 let ...Rd8 and ...Nd3 infiltrate; evaluation fell from 54% to 44%

[middlegame] Deny enemy knights the d3/c2/f3 outposts: control them with a rook, bishop or pawn (c3, Be3) before the knight arrives, not after Example: Black's ...Nd3 repeatedly harassed my rook and queen because no piece covered d3

[middlegame] If two enemy knights attack one pawn defended only by your queen, add a defender with a knight or advance the pawn; a queen-only guard invites Nxd3 removal tactics Example: d3 was hit by Nb4 and Nc5 with just Qd1 guarding, forcing awkward bishop moves

[middlegame] Before every move, list your undefended pieces and the squares where one enemy move can hit two of them; fix the loosest one first Example: Bishop on d5/e4 plus pawn d3 both loose gave Black tempo moves ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5

[middlegame] When your bishop pair is deep in enemy territory on light squares, keep a pawn or knight supporting the outpost, else the bishop is just a target Example: Bd5 and Be4 were both chased by pawns because c4/d3 support never came

[endgame] With an extra pawn and rooks on, activate the rook behind or beside the passer and trade off the opponent's active knight before advancing Example: After c5 my passer went nowhere while Black's knight on d3/b3 tied my pieces down

[endgame] Before simplifying into a pawn-up ending, check the opponent's knight cannot reach a fork square near your rook and king; trade knights if it can Example: Nxc5/Nb3 kept forking ideas alive and nearly equalized a winning position

[middlegame] Convert an attack by looking for back-rank and last-rank rook invasions (R to 8th) once the opponent's pieces drift to one wing Example: 24.Rd8 worked only because Black's knight was on b3 and queen on a6, far from the king
[opening] In the Spanish with Ba4/Bb3, delay flank pawn pushes (a4) until Nc3 or d3/c3 is in and e4 has two defenders Example: 8.a4 came before Nc3/Nbd2 and the resulting trades cost the e4 pawn

[middlegame] Compare candidate moves by asking "what is my opponent's best reply pawn push?" before deciding; if a pawn push gains a tempo on you, pick another move Example: ...d5 and ...f5 both gained tempo on Be4; checking pawn pushes first would have revealed Nc3
